title: Turn messy meeting notes into clear actions
hook: You have 40 minutes of notes and no idea what anyone agreed to.
problem: Notes from a meeting are rarely written in an order that shows who must do what.
steps: Paste your own rough notes (remove names of customers and any company data).
Ask for decisions, actions with an owner, and open questions, in three separate lists.
Read it against your notes and fix anything it guessed.
prompt: Here are my rough meeting notes: [paste notes]. List (1) decisions made, (2) actions with an owner and a due date if stated, (3) open questions. If something is not stated, write 'not stated' instead of guessing.
checks: Every owner and date appears in your original notes.
Nothing is listed as decided that was only discussed.
mistake: Letting the AI fill gaps with names or dates it made up.
privacy: Do not paste customer or company data into an AI tool.

title: Draft a reply in your own tone, then make it yours
hook: A tricky email sits in your inbox because you cannot find the right tone.
problem: A first draft in the right tone is quicker to edit than a blank page.
steps: Paste the email you received (no customer data) and say what you want to happen.
Give two or three words for the tone, such as 'warm, brief, firm'.
Edit the draft until it sounds like you, then send it yourself.
prompt: Here is an email I received: [paste]. Write a short reply that does this: [your aim]. Tone: [warm, brief, firm]. Do not promise anything I have not listed here: [list].
checks: It promises nothing you did not agree to.
Names, dates and figures match the original email.
privacy: Do not paste customer or company data into an AI tool.

title: Summarise a long document without losing the detail that matters
hook: A 30-page report lands on your desk an hour before the meeting.
problem: A summary is only useful if you can check it against the source.
steps: Paste or upload the document if your organisation allows it for this tool.
Ask for a summary with the section or page each point came from.
Open the original at those points and confirm the three that matter most.
prompt: Summarise this document in 8 bullet points for a busy manager: [paste text]. After each point, give the section heading or page it came from. Then list 3 questions the document does not answer.
checks: Check the three most important points against the source.
Look for numbers: confirm each one in the document.
mistake: Trusting a summary of a document you have not opened.
privacy: Do not paste customer or company data into an AI tool.

title: Get an Excel formula you can actually test
hook: You know what you want the spreadsheet to do but not how to write the formula.
problem: Describing the result you want beats guessing at function names.
steps: Describe your columns and one example row (fake or anonymised values).
Say what the formula should return, in one sentence.
Test it on three rows where you already know the answer.
prompt: My sheet has these columns: [letter: what it holds, for example A: date, B: type, C: amount]. In [cell] I want [the result, for example the total of C where B is 'Retail']. Give me an Excel formula for [cell] and explain it in one sentence.
checks: It works on three rows whose answers you know.
It still works when a cell is blank.
mistake: Pasting real customer rows to 'show' the data.
privacy: Do not paste customer or company data into an AI tool.

title: Clean a messy list into a tidy table
hook: A copied list has mixed formats, odd spacing and duplicates.
problem: Cleaning by hand is slow and easy to get wrong; checking is quicker.
steps: Use a small sample with no personal or customer data.
Say the columns you want and how to treat blanks and duplicates.
Count the rows before and after.
prompt: Turn this list into a table with columns Name, Date (DD/MM/YYYY), Amount (GBP). Keep every row. If a value is missing write 'blank'. List any rows you were unsure about at the end: [paste sample]
checks: The row count is the same, or you can explain the difference.
The 'unsure' rows were checked by you.
mistake: Letting the AI quietly drop rows.
privacy: Do not paste customer or company data into an AI tool.

title: Prepare better questions for a meeting
hook: You walk into a meeting knowing the agenda but not what to ask.
problem: Good questions come from the gaps in what you already know.
steps: Write what you know and what you are trying to decide.
Ask for questions that would change the decision, not generic ones.
Pick the three you could not answer yourself.
prompt: I am meeting [role] to decide [decision]. What I already know: [3 facts]. Suggest 8 questions that would change my decision if the answer were surprising, and say why each one matters.
checks: Each question ties to the decision you actually face.
You can say what answer would change your mind.
mistake: Using a long list of generic questions.
privacy: Do not paste customer or company data into an AI tool.

title: Explain a hard idea at three levels
hook: You need to explain something technical to a mixed audience.
problem: One idea told three ways reaches more people.
steps: Name the idea and the audience.
Ask for a one-line version, a paragraph, and a version with an example.
Keep the version that suits the room and check the facts.
prompt: Explain [idea] three ways: (1) one sentence for a busy executive, (2) one paragraph for a new colleague, (3) a short version with a real-world example. Do not use jargon without explaining it.
checks: The technical details are still correct.
The example matches your real situation.
mistake: Using the simple version without checking what it left out.
privacy: Do not paste customer or company data into an AI tool.

title: Tighten your writing without losing your voice
hook: Your draft is too long and you can no longer see what to cut.
problem: Cutting is easier when you can compare before and after.
steps: Paste your own draft.
Ask for a version 20 percent shorter that keeps your phrasing.
Compare the two and keep only the cuts you like.
prompt: Here is my draft: [paste]. Make it about 20 percent shorter. Keep my wording and tone where you can. Show what you removed in a separate list so I can put anything back.
checks: Your key point is still there.
It still sounds like you.
privacy: Do not paste customer or company data into an AI tool.

title: Compare options with a table you can defend
hook: You have three options and a gut feeling.
problem: A table of criteria shows what you are really weighing.
steps: List the options and what matters to you.
Ask for a table scored against your criteria, with assumptions stated.
Change the assumptions you disagree with and re-run it.
prompt: Compare these options: [A, B, C]. My criteria, in order of importance: [list]. Make a table with a short reason for each score and list the assumptions you made.
checks: You agree with each assumption listed.
The ranking changes if you change the order of your criteria.
mistake: Treating the AI's scores as facts.
privacy: Do not paste customer or company data into an AI tool.

title: Break a vague task into a plan with risks
hook: 'Improve the onboarding process' is not yet a plan.
problem: A first plan gives you something to correct.
steps: Describe the goal, the deadline and who is involved.
Ask for steps, who does each, and the three biggest risks.
Edit it with what you know about your team.
prompt: Goal: [goal]. Deadline: [date]. People: [roles]. Break this into 6 to 10 steps with a suggested owner for each, and list the 3 biggest risks with one way to reduce each.
checks: Every step is something your team can actually do.
The risks are real ones for your situation.
mistake: Following the plan without adjusting it.
privacy: Do not paste customer or company data into an AI tool.
